```{r}
#| echo: false
library(tidyverse)
```

### Chocolate Candy Performance

For this project, I wanted to look at whether chocolate candies perform better than candies without chocolate. I personally think the best candies contain chocolate and peanuts, so I was interested in seeing whether chocolate was associated with candy popularity. I used the FiveThirtyEight candy dataset, where each row represents a candy and the columns describe its different attributes. The win percentage represents how often a candy was chosen when participants were presented with two candy options.

My null hypothesis is that chocolate content and win percentage are not associated. My alternative hypothesis is that chocolate candies have a higher average win percentage than non-chocolate candies. I will use a permutation test to simulate the null hypothesis and see whether the observed difference is unusual.

```{r}
candy <- read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fivethirtyeight/data/master/candy-power-ranking/candy-data.csv"
)

candy <- candy |>
  mutate(chocolate = if_else(chocolate == 1, "Yes", "No"))

candy |>
  select(chocolate, winpercent) |>
  head()
```

First, I made a boxplot to compare the win percentages of chocolate and non-chocolate candies. This allows us to see the difference in the distributions before running the simulation. Each group contains candies with a range of win percentages, but I am especially interested in comparing their averages.

```{r}
candy |>
  ggplot(aes(x = chocolate, y = winpercent)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#2A0081", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Chocolate Candy Performance",
    x = "Contains Chocolate",
    y = "Win Percentage"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Helvetica Neue") +
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = 14, color = "#2A0081")
  )
```

### Difference in Mean Win Percentage

Next, I calculated the mean win percentage for chocolate and non-chocolate candies. Chocolate candies had an average win percentage of approximately 60.9%, while non-chocolate candies had an average of approximately 42.1%. This gives an observed difference of about 18.8 percentage points. I want to see whether this difference could reasonably occur if chocolate content and win percentage were unrelated.

```{r}
candy |>
  group_by(chocolate) |>
  summarize(mean_win = mean(winpercent))

observed_diff <- candy |>
  summarize(
    diff = mean(winpercent[chocolate == "Yes"]) -
           mean(winpercent[chocolate == "No"])
  ) |>
  pull(diff)

observed_diff
```

### Permutation Simulation

To test the null hypothesis, I wrote a function called `shuffle_test()`. This function randomly shuffles the win percentages while keeping the chocolate Yes/No labels the same. It then calculates the average shuffled win percentage for both groups and returns the difference between their means. By shuffling the percentages, I am simulating what the difference could look like if there were no association between chocolate content and win percentage.

```{r}
shuffle_test <- function() {

  shuffled <- candy |>
    mutate(shuffled_percent = sample(winpercent,
                                     size = 85,
                                     replace = FALSE))

  diff <- shuffled |>
    summarize(
      diff = mean(shuffled_percent[chocolate == "Yes"]) -
             mean(shuffled_percent[chocolate == "No"])
    ) |>
    pull(diff)

  return(diff)
}
```

I then used `map_dbl()` to run my function 5,000 times. I chose `map_dbl()` because my function returns one numerical value each time, which is the difference in means from one shuffle. I stored the results in a tibble so I could visualize the distribution of simulated differences.

```{r}
set.seed(123)

simulations <- tibble(
  diff = map_dbl(1:5000, ~ shuffle_test())
)

head(simulations)
```

### Null Distribution of Candy Popularity

I made a histogram to visualize the 5,000 simulated differences in mean win percentage. The purple bars show the differences that occurred under the null hypothesis, and the pink line represents the observed difference from the original data. The simulated differences should be centered around zero because the null hypothesis assumes that chocolate content and win percentage are unrelated.

```{r}
simulations |>
  ggplot(aes(x = diff)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 30,
    fill = "#2A0081",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = observed_diff,
    color = "#BA1780",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Null Distribution of Candy Win Percentages",
    subtitle = "5,000 Permutations Under the Null Hypothesis",
    x = "Difference in Mean Win Percentage (Yes - No)",
    y = "Number of Simulations",
    caption = "Pink line represents the observed difference"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Helvetica Neue") +
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = 14, color = "#2A0081")
  )
```

### P-Value and Results

To calculate the p-value, I found the proportion of simulated differences that were greater than or equal to the observed difference. Because my alternative hypothesis is that chocolate candies perform better, I used a right-tailed test. None of my 5,000 simulations produced a difference as large as the observed difference, giving me a simulated p-value of zero. This does not mean the true p-value is exactly zero, but it suggests that the observed difference is extremely unlikely under the null hypothesis.

```{r}
p_value <- simulations |>
  summarize(p = mean(diff >= observed_diff)) |>
  pull(p)

p_value
```

### Conclusion

For this project, I investigated whether chocolate candies have higher average win percentages than non-chocolate candies. I wrote a function to randomly shuffle win percentages and used `map_dbl()` to repeat the simulation 5,000 times. My observed difference was approximately 18.8 percentage points, and none of my simulations produced a difference as large as the original, giving a simulated p-value of zero (which I report as p < 0.0002). This provides strong evidence of an association between chocolate content and win percentage among these 85 candies, although the data do not establish causation or necessarily represent the preferences of all candy consumers.

### About the Data

For this project, I used the Halloween Candy Power Ranking dataset from FiveThirtyEight. The original data came from an online survey in which participants chose their preferred candy in head-to-head matchups. The dataset includes 85 candies and information about their ingredients, characteristics, and win percentages.

**Source:** [FiveThirtyEight Candy Power Ranking Dataset](https://github.com/fivethirtyeight/data/tree/master/candy-power-ranking)

**Original data:** Walt Hickey, *The Ultimate Halloween Candy Power Ranking*, FiveThirtyEight (2017).
